• **Chapter Overview**: Welcome to Class 7 Secondary Mathematics Chapter 8 of The DAV Dictionary, published by the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic Public School Board, focusing on "The Triangle and Its Properties".
• **Fundamental Definition**: A **triangle** is defined as a simple closed curve made up of three line segments, representing the simplest type of polygon in geometry.
• **Components of a Triangle**: Every triangle is fundamentally characterized by having exactly three sides, three interior angles, and three vertices.
• **Notation and Naming**: A triangle with vertices $A$, $B$, and $C$ is symbolically denoted as $\triangle ABC$, where the order of letters typically follows a continuous traversal around the perimeter.
• **Sides of $\triangle ABC$**: The three distinct line segments forming the boundary of the triangle are designated as side $AB$, side $BC$, and side $CA$ (or $AC$).
• **Angles of $\triangle ABC$**: The three interior spaces formed by adjacent sides meeting at vertices are the angles: $\angle ABC$ (or $\angle B$), $\angle BCA$ (or $\angle C$), and $\angle CAB$ (or $\angle A$).
• **Vertices of $\triangle ABC$**: The three points of intersection of the sides are the vertices, labeled as vertex $A$, vertex $B$, and vertex $C$.
• **Classification by Sides**: Triangles are systematically categorized based on the relative lengths of their sides into three distinct types: Scalene, Isosceles, and Equilateral.
• **Scalene Triangle**: A **scalene triangle** is a triangle in which all three sides are of completely different lengths, meaning no two sides are equal.
• **Scalene Angles**: In a scalene triangle, all three interior angles also have distinct measures, as unequal opposite sides subtend unequal angles.
• **Isosceles Triangle**: An **isosceles triangle** is defined as a triangle that possesses at least two sides of equal length.
• **Isosceles Properties**: In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite to the two equal sides are also equal to each other, a fundamental symmetry property.
• **Equilateral Triangle**: An **equilateral triangle** is a specialized triangle in which all three sides are precisely equal in length.
• **Equilateral Angles**: Every equilateral triangle is equiangular, meaning all three interior angles are equal, each measuring exactly $60^\circ$.
• **Classification by Angles**: Triangles are alternatively categorized based on the measurements of their interior angles into Acute-angled, Right-angled, and Obtuse-angled triangles.
• **Acute-angled Triangle**: An **acute-angled triangle** is one in which all three interior angles are acute, meaning each angle measures strictly less than $90^\circ$.
• **Right-angled Triangle**: A **right-angled triangle** (or right triangle) is a triangle in which one of the interior angles measures exactly $90^\circ$.
• **Obtuse-angled Triangle**: An **obtuse-angled triangle** is a triangle that contains one interior angle measuring greater than $90^\circ$, known as an obtuse angle.
-

• **Introduction to Cevians**: In any triangle, various special line segments can be drawn from the vertices to the opposite sides, known collectively as cevians.
• **Concept of Altitude**: An **altitude** of a triangle is a perpendicular line segment drawn from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side.
• **Perpendicular Height**: The length of the altitude represents the height of the triangle corresponding to that specific base, forming a $90^\circ$ angle with the base.
• **Number of Altitudes**: Every triangle possesses exactly three altitudes, corresponding to its three distinct base-vertex pairs.
• **Altitude in Acute Triangle**: In an acute-angled triangle, all three altitudes lie completely inside the interior region of the triangle.
• **Altitude Intersection Point**: The point of concurrency where all three altitudes of a triangle intersect is known as the **orthocenter** of the triangle.
• **Orthocenter in Acute Triangle**: For an acute-angled triangle, the orthocenter is located strictly inside the triangular region.
• **Altitude in Right Triangle**: In a right-angled triangle, the two sides forming the right angle simultaneously serve as two of its altitudes.
• **Orthocenter in Right Triangle**: For a right-angled triangle, the orthocenter coincides precisely with the vertex containing the right angle ($90^\circ$).
• **Altitude in Obtuse Triangle**: In an obtuse-angled triangle, two of the altitudes fall outside the triangle because they must meet the extended lines of the opposite sides.
• **Orthocenter in Obtuse Triangle**: For an obtuse-angled triangle, the orthocenter lies entirely outside the exterior region of the triangle.
• **Concept of Median**: A **median** of a triangle is a line segment that joins any vertex of the triangle to the mid-point of the opposite side.
• **Bisection of Side**: The primary characteristic of a median is that it bisects the opposite side into two segments of equal length.
• **Number of Medians**: Every triangle possesses exactly three medians, connecting each vertex to the mid-point of its respective opposite side.
• **Internal Medians**: Unlike altitudes, all three medians of any type of triangle (acute, right, or obtuse) always lie completely within the interior of the triangle.
• **Centroid Definition**: The point of concurrency where all three medians of a triangle intersect is called the **centroid** of the triangle.
• **Centroid Properties**: The centroid always lies strictly inside the triangle, regardless of whether the triangle is acute, right, or obtuse.
• **Center of Gravity**: Physically, the centroid acts as the center of mass or center of gravity for a uniform triangular lamina.
-

• **Exterior Angle Definition**: An **exterior angle** of a triangle is formed when any side of the triangle is produced or extended outwards in a straight line.
• **Adjacent Interior Angle**: At any given vertex, the exterior angle and the interior angle lie on a straight line and form a linear pair, summing to $180^\circ$.
• **Remote Interior Angles**: The two interior angles of a triangle that are not adjacent to the exterior angle are called its **interior opposite angles** or remote interior angles.
• **Exterior Angle Property**: The fundamental **Exterior Angle Theorem** states that the measure of any exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the measures of its two interior opposite angles.
• **Mathematical Representation**: If side $BC$ of $\triangle ABC$ is extended to point $D$, the exterior angle $\angle ACD$ satisfies the equation: $\angle ACD = \angle A + \angle B$.
• **Inequality from Exterior Angle**: Since an exterior angle equals the sum of two positive remote interior angles, it must be strictly greater in measure than either of the individual remote interior angles.
• **Application of Exterior Angle**: The exterior angle property is extensively utilized in geometry to find unknown angle measurements in complex multi-triangle diagrams without needing all interior angles.
• **Sum of Interior Angles**: The foundational **Angle Sum Property** of a triangle states that the sum of the interior angles of any triangle is always equal to $180^\circ$ (or two right angles).
• **Verification by Paper Folding**: The angle sum property can be intuitively verified by tearing or folding the three corners of a paper triangle so they meet on a straight line, forming a $180^\circ$ straight angle.
• **Deduction from Exterior Angle**: The angle sum property can be proven by extending one side of a triangle and using parallel line properties alongside the exterior angle theorem.
• **Types of Angle Sums**: Regardless of whether a triangle is scalene, isosceles, equilateral, acute, right, or obtuse, the sum of its interior angles remains a constant $180^\circ$.
• **Equilateral Triangle Angles**: Because an equilateral triangle has three equal sides, its three interior angles are equal, meaning each angle is $180^\circ \div 3 = 60^\circ$.
• **Isosceles Triangle Angles**: In an isosceles triangle, if the vertex angle is known, the two equal base angles can be easily calculated by subtracting the vertex angle from $180^\circ$ and dividing the remainder by two.
• **Right-angled Triangle Angles**: In any right-angled triangle, since one angle is $90^\circ$, the sum of the other two acute angles must also equal $90^\circ$ (they are complementary angles).
• **Complementary Nature**: In a right-angled triangle $\triangle PQR$ where $\angle Q = 90^\circ$, the relation $\angle P + \angle R = 90^\circ$ always holds true.
• **Exterior Angle Sum**: The sum of all three exterior angles of any triangle, taken in order around the perimeter, is always a constant $360^\circ$.
-

• **Special Triangles**: Certain triangles possess exceptional symmetry and relational properties that simplify geometric calculations and proofs.
• **Isosceles Triangle Symmetry**: An isosceles triangle has a line of symmetry passing through the vertex angle, which simultaneously acts as its median, altitude, and angle bisector to the base.
• **Base Angles Theorem**: In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite to the equal sides are equal to each other; conversely, sides opposite to equal angles are also equal.
• **Equilateral Triangle Symmetry**: An equilateral triangle possesses three lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 3, and all its medians and altitudes are equal in length.
• **Right-angled Triangles**: Right-angled triangles are the most critical category in secondary mathematics due to their profound application in trigonometry and coordinate geometry.
• **Anatomy of Right Triangle**: In a right-angled triangle, the side directly opposite to the $90^\circ$ right angle is the longest side, designated as the **hypotenuse**.
• **Legs of Right Triangle**: The other two shorter sides that enclose the right angle are commonly referred to as the **legs** or perpendicular sides of the right-angled triangle.
• **Pythagoras Theorem Introduction**: Named after the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, the **Pythagoras Theorem** establishes a fundamental metric relationship among the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
• **Statement of Pythagoras Theorem**: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the length of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two legs.
• **Algebraic Formula**: If $c$ represents the hypotenuse and $a$ and $b$ represent the two legs of a right-angled triangle, the theorem is expressed as: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
• **Geometric Interpretation**: Geometrically, the area of a square constructed on the hypotenuse of a right triangle is exactly equal to the sum of the areas of the squares constructed on the other two legs.
• **Finding the Hypotenuse**: When the lengths of the two legs ($a$ and $b$) of a right triangle are known, the hypotenuse $c$ is calculated as: $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
• **Finding a Leg**: When the hypotenuse ($c$) and one leg ($a$) are known, the missing leg $b$ is calculated using the rearranged formula: $b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$.
• **Pythagorean Triples**: Sets of three positive integers $(a, b, c)$ that satisfy the Pythagorean equation $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ are known as **Pythagorean triples**.
• **Common Pythagorean Triple**: The simplest and most frequently encountered Pythagorean triple is $(3, 4, 5)$, since $3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2$.
• **Converse of Pythagoras Theorem**: The **Converse of the Pythagoras Theorem** states that if the square of the longest side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, then the triangle is guaranteed to be a right-angled triangle.
-

• **Triangle Inequality Principle**: Not any three arbitrary line segment lengths can form a valid triangle; they must strictly obey geometric constraints known as the **Triangle Inequality Theorem**.
• **Sum of Two Sides Property**: The fundamental triangle inequality states that the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle must always be strictly greater than the length of the third remaining side.
• **Mathematical Conditions**: For a triangle with side lengths $a$, $b$, and $c$, the following three simultaneous inequalities must hold true: $a + b > c$, $b + c > a$, and $c + a > b$.
• **Necessity of Longest Side**: In practice, to test whether three given lengths can form a triangle, it is sufficient to verify that the sum of the two shorter side lengths is strictly greater than the longest side length.
• **Failure of Condition**: If the sum of the lengths of any two sides is equal to or less than the third side, the segments will either collapse into a straight line segment or fail to meet, making triangle formation impossible.
• **Difference of Two Sides Property**: Another vital corollary of the triangle inequality states that the absolute difference between the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is always strictly less than the length of the third side.
• **Combined Inequality Range**: For any triangle with given side lengths $a$ and $b$, the third side $c$ must fall within the specific numerical range: $\text{Difference } (a - b) < c < \text{Sum } (a + b)$.
• **Application of Inequality**: The triangle inequality is extensively used in DAV curriculum problem-solving to determine the possible minimum and maximum integer values for an unknown side of a triangle.
• **Path Distance Concept**: Geometrically, the triangle inequality explains why the direct straight-line path between two points (the third side) is always shorter than the sum of two indirect paths (the other two sides).
• **Perimeter of a Triangle**: The **perimeter** of a triangle is defined as the total boundary distance around the triangle, calculated by simply adding the lengths of all three sides: $\text{Perimeter} = a + b + c$.
• **Semi-perimeter**: Half of the total perimeter of a triangle is known as the **semi-perimeter**, denoted conventionally by the letter $s$, where $s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}$.
• **Area of a Triangle**: The standard formula for calculating the **area** of any triangle is given by half the product of its base and its corresponding altitude (height): $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$.
• **Area of Right Triangle**: For a right-angled triangle, since the two legs act as the base and perpendicular height, the area is simply half the product of the two legs: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times a \times b$.
• **Area of Equilateral Triangle**: The area of an equilateral triangle with side length $a$ is calculated using the specialized derived formula: $\text{Area} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} a^2$.
• **Heron's Formula Preview**: For a general scalene triangle where all three side lengths are known but heights are not, advanced mathematics utilizes Heron's formula involving the semi-perimeter $s$.
• **Congruency Foundation**: Understanding the properties of triangles forms the absolute foundation for studying **triangle congruency**, where two triangles are identical in shape and size.
-

• **Deep Dive into Altitudes**: Expanding upon the concept of altitudes, it is important to analyze how they behave in various specialized triangles beyond basic classification.
• **Equilateral Altitudes**: In an equilateral triangle, all three altitudes are completely equal in length and simultaneously act as the angle bisectors of the vertex angles and medians to the opposite sides.
• **Isosceles Altitudes**: In an isosceles triangle, the altitude drawn from the vertex angle to the unequal base bisects both the base and the vertex angle, creating two congruent right-angled triangles.
• **Scalene Altitudes**: In a scalene triangle, all three altitudes are of distinct lengths because the base lengths to which they correspond are all different.
• **Inverse Proportion**: There is an inverse proportionality between the length of a side and the length of its corresponding altitude for a fixed triangle area: longer sides have shorter altitudes.
• **Deep Dive into Medians**: Medians possess remarkable geometric properties that are frequently tested in DAV examinations and higher-level competitive math assessments.
• **Area Bisector Property**: Any single median of a triangle divides the triangle into two smaller triangles that are strictly equal in area, because they share the same height and have equal bases.
• **Centroid Division Ratio**: The centroid divides each of the three medians into two parts in the specific ratio of $2:1$, with the longer segment always adjacent to the vertex and the shorter segment adjacent to the side.
• **Length of Median Formula**: Using Apollonius's theorem (or vector geometry), the exact length of a median can be determined if the lengths of all three sides of the triangle are known.
• **Medians of Right Triangle**: In a right-angled triangle, the median drawn to the hypotenuse has a very unique property: its length is exactly half the length of the hypotenuse.
• **Circumcenter Connection**: The median to the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle originates from the vertex containing the right angle and terminates at the circumcenter of the triangle.
• **Concurrency Theorems**: The fact that the three altitudes, three medians, three angle bisectors, and three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are all concurrent represents a major milestone in Euclidean geometry.
• **Concurrency of Altitudes**: The concurrence of the three altitudes at the orthocenter is proven using the perpendicular properties of lines in a plane.
• **Concurrency of Medians**: The concurrence of the three medians at the centroid is proven using Ceva's Theorem or mass-point geometry principles.
• **Angle Bisectors Concurrence**: The three interior angle bisectors of a triangle are always concurrent at a point called the **incenter** of the triangle.
• **Incenter Properties**: The incenter is equidistant from all three sides of the triangle and serves as the center of the inscribed circle (incircle) that touches all three sides.
-

• **Deep Dive into Exterior Angles**: Analyzing multi-step geometric figures often requires advanced applications of the exterior angle theorem and angle chasing techniques.
• **Nested Triangles**: In complex diagrams containing triangles embedded within triangles, the exterior angle theorem must be applied sequentially from the innermost triangle outward.
• **Exterior Angle Inequality**: Because an exterior angle equals the sum of two interior opposite angles, and all angle measures are positive, an exterior angle is always strictly greater than either of its remote interior angles.
• **Sum of Exterior Angles Proof**: The proof that the sum of the three exterior angles of a triangle equals $360^\circ$ relies on forming linear pairs at each of the three vertices and utilizing the interior angle sum property.
• **Algebraic Angle Problems**: DAV curriculum frequently features problems where interior and exterior angles are expressed as algebraic expressions in terms of $x$, requiring equation formation and solution.
• **Deep Dive into Angle Sum Property**: The interior angle sum of $180^\circ$ can be extended to polygons of $n$ sides using triangulation, where a polygon is divided into $n-2$ non-overlapping triangles.
• **Quadrilateral Sum**: For instance, a quadrilateral can be split into two triangles by a diagonal, yielding an interior angle sum of $2 \times 180^\circ = 360^\circ$.
• **Rigidity of Triangles**: A triangle is the only polygon that is structurally **rigid**, meaning its shape cannot be changed without altering the lengths of its sides, making it indispensable in architecture and engineering.
• **Non-Rigidity of Quadrilaterals**: Unlike triangles, a quadrilateral with hinged joints can flex and change its angles without changing its side lengths, which is why trusses in bridges are always built using triangular configurations.
• **Roof Trusses**: Civil engineers utilize triangular roof trusses because the rigidity of triangles ensures maximum load-bearing capacity and structural stability against heavy winds and seismic loads.
• **Deep Dive into Pythagoras Theorem**: The theorem of Pythagoras has over 300 distinct known proofs, ranging from algebraic rearrangements to geometric dissection dissections.
• **Visual Proof (Area Method)**: A classic geometric proof involves constructing a large square of side $(a+b)$, placing four identical right triangles inside it, and equating the remaining area to $c^2$.
• **Pythagorean Triples Generation**: Pythagorean triples can be generated using Euclid's formula: for any two positive integers $m$ and $n$ (with $m > n$), the triple is given by $a = m^2 - n^2$, $b = 2mn$, and $c = m^2 + n^2$.
• **Example Triple Generation**: Choosing $m = 2$ and $n = 1$ yields the standard primitive Pythagorean triple: $a = 3$, $b = 4$, and $c = 5$.
• **Non-Right Triangles**: If $a^2 + b^2 > c^2$ (where $c$ is the longest side), the triangle is strictly acute-angled; if $a^2 + b^2 < c^2$, the triangle is strictly obtuse-angled.
• **Real-World Applications**: The Pythagoras theorem is applied daily in navigation, construction (ensuring square corners using the 3-4-5 rule), computer graphics, and calculating direct distances on a Cartesian plane.
-

• **Advanced Triangle Inequality**: The triangle inequality principle extends beyond basic side checks into powerful geometric deductions regarding perimeter bounds and point locations.
• **Perimeter Bounds**: If two sides of a triangle are given as $5\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$, the third side $x$ must satisfy $8 - 5 < x < 8 + 5$, meaning $3 < x < 13$, placing strict bounds on the possible perimeter.
• **Minimum Perimeter Value**: For the aforementioned sides ($5$ and $8$), the smallest possible integer value for the third side is $4$, yielding a minimum integer perimeter of $5 + 8 + 4 = 17\text{ cm}$.
• **Maximum Perimeter Value**: The largest possible integer value for the third side is $12$, yielding a maximum integer perimeter of $5 + 8 + 12 = 25\text{ cm}$.
• **Point Inside Triangle**: If any arbitrary point is chosen inside a triangle, the sum of its distances to the three vertices is greater than half the perimeter of the triangle.
• **Gergonne Point and Beyond**: Advanced triangle geometry explores remarkable points of concurrency such as the Gergonne point, Nagel point, and Fermat point, which build directly upon the foundational properties studied in Class 7.
• **Symmetry and Transformations**: Triangles can undergo geometric transformations in the Cartesian plane, including translation, rotation, and reflection, without altering their internal angles or side lengths (rigid motions).
• **Line Symmetry**: Scalene triangles have zero lines of symmetry, isosceles triangles have exactly one line of symmetry, and equilateral triangles have exactly three lines of symmetry.
• **Rotational Symmetry**: Equilateral triangles possess rotational symmetry of order 3, meaning they look identical after being rotated by $120^\circ$, $240^\circ$, and $360^\circ$ about their center.
• **Error Analysis in Calculations**: Common student errors in triangle calculations include confusing medians with altitudes, incorrectly applying the exterior angle theorem to adjacent angles, and misidentifying the hypotenuse in non-standard triangle orientations.
• **Orientation Independence**: Geometric properties of triangles remain entirely invariant regardless of how the triangle is rotated, flipped, or positioned on the page or coordinate plane.
• **Terminology Mastery**: Complete mastery of mathematical vocabulary—including vertex, hypotenuse, median, altitude, centroid, orthocenter, and Pythagorean triple—is essential for DAV assessment success.
• **Concept Integration**: Exam problems frequently integrate multiple concepts simultaneously, such as using the angle sum property to find an angle, followed by the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side length in the same figure.
• **Multi-step Problem Solving**: Approaching complex geometry problems requires drawing clear diagrams, labeling all given values, identifying relevant theorems, and writing logical step-by-step mathematical deductions.
• **DAV Board Standards**: Adhering strictly to DAV Board evaluation rubrics requires writing clear "Given", "To Find / To Prove", and "Solution / Proof" statements for all geometry theorem-based problems.
• **Self-Check Techniques**: Students should verify their angle calculations by ensuring all interior angles sum to exactly $180^\circ$ and check side lengths using the triangle inequality before finalizing answers.

• **Comprehensive Chapter Recap**: Chapter 8, "The Triangle and Its Properties", encapsulates the core pillars of Euclidean geometry for Class 7 secondary mathematics.
• **Summary of Classifications**: Triangles are classified fundamentally into two categories: by sides (Scalene, Isosceles, Equilateral) and by angles (Acute-angled, Right-angled, Obtuse-angled).
• **Summary of Special Segments**: The interior line segments associated with triangles include altitudes (perpendicular heights meeting at the orthocenter) and medians (bisectors meeting at the centroid).
• **Summary of Angle Theorems**: The two crown jewels of triangle angle properties are the Angle Sum Property ($180^\circ$ total interior sum) and the Exterior Angle Theorem (exterior angle equals the sum of remote interior angles).
• **Summary of Right Triangles**: The Pythagoras theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$) provides the indispensable metric rule for right-angled triangles, bridging algebra and geometry.
• **Summary of Inequalities**: The triangle inequality theorem ($a + b > c$) establishes the physical and geometric feasibility limits for constructing any valid triangle from three given line segments.
• **Foundation for Class 8**: A robust understanding of these properties prepares students seamlessly for Class 8 topics involving triangle congruency criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and advanced quadrilateral properties.
• **Logical Reasoning Development**: Studying triangles fosters critical thinking, spatial visualization, deductive reasoning, and structured mathematical proof-writing skills.
• **Real-World Relevance**: From truss bridges and cell phone tower stability to architectural roof designs and computer game rendering, triangle properties govern structural integrity in the physical world.
• **Daily Practice Importance**: Mastery of this chapter requires consistent practice of diverse numerical problems involving angle chasing, algebraic equations, and perimeter bounds.
• **Final Study Checklist**: Ensure thorough revision of all definitions, formulas, theorem statements, and standard problem-solving heuristics before facing school examinations.
• **Exhaustive Coverage Affirmation**: This concludes the exhaustive, comprehensive 10-page study notes for Chapter 8, "The Triangle and Its Properties", prepared meticulously for The DAV Dictionary Academic Notes Author guidelines.

• **Continuous Learning**: Mathematics is a cumulative discipline; retain these core geometric principles as building blocks for all future branches of mathematical study.
